name: Sun exposure for acne
lead: Sun exposure for acne is the practice of tanning or sitting in sunlight in the belief that it dries out blemishes. Community members sometimes report a short-term improvement in appearance.

General acne references state that sunlight exposure is not associated with acne overall, that intense UVA can trigger a separate eruption called acne aestivalis, and that sun exposure can prolong postinflammatory hyperpigmentation, for which daily sunscreen is advised [1]. A study of acne patients also examined the link between postinflammatory hyperpigmentation and melasma [2].
infobox: Drying and temporary clearing of blemishes

paras: Proponents say sun makes spots look drier and less inflamed for a time. Wikipedia reports that sunlight is not generally associated with acne [1].

Wikipedia notes that sun exposure can sustain postinflammatory hyperpigmentation and that daily SPF 15 or higher sunscreen can reduce that risk [1]. Acne aestivalis, a UVA-triggered polymorphous light eruption, typically appears on the arms, shoulders, back and chest and spares the face [1]. An Iranian study compared melasma and postinflammatory hyperpigmentation in acne patients [2].
No studies found specifically testing tanning as an acne treatment. Related work on pigmentation in acne patients exists [2].

card.summary: Tanning to dry out spots; reference sources link sun to lingering dark marks rather than clearer skin.
card.note: Sun can prolong post-acne pigmentation per general references.

quick.overview:
Some people tan or sunbathe in the hope of drying out acne. The effect, when reported, is described as temporary.

General references say sunlight is not associated with acne overall but can sustain post-acne dark marks.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say UV makes blemishes look drier and less red; no published trial supports it as a treatment.
quick.risks: UV can sustain postinflammatory hyperpigmentation, and intense UVA can trigger acne aestivalis; sunscreen is advised by references.
